red_flags.text: Pain out of proportion, spreading erythema or crepitus over the perineum, scrotum or labia, skin necrosis, or systemic toxicity: Fournier's gangrene, which needs theatre within hours.
Diabetes, immunosuppression, neutropenia or HIV with perianal pain: sepsis spreads faster and signs are blunted.
Deep rectal pain with fever but little to see externally: intersphincteric or supralevator abscess, which needs an examination under anaesthesia or imaging.
Atypical fissure (lateral, multiple, painless or large) or recurrent complex sepsis: think Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, HIV, sexually transmitted infection or malignancy.

do_now.text: Perianal abscess: prompt incision and drainage. Do not wait for fluctuance and do not treat with antibiotics alone.
Add antibiotics only for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, or immunosuppression, and in patients with relevant prosthetic or valvular risk per local protocol.
Suspected Fournier's gangrene: resuscitate, broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol and emergency surgical debridement.
Thrombosed external haemorrhoid presenting early, within about 72 hours of onset: consider excision of the thrombosed haemorrhoid under local anaesthetic rather than incision of the clot.
Acute pilonidal abscess: incision and drainage, with definitive treatment of the sinus planned later once the acute sepsis has settled.

assess.text: Inspect and palpate the perineum, buttocks and genitalia; check for tenderness above the dentate line on rectal examination.
Screen for systemic sepsis and necrotising infection.
Check capillary glucose: new or poorly controlled diabetes is common in perianal sepsis and in Fournier's gangrene.
History of bowel habit, previous abscesses, weight loss and family history of inflammatory bowel disease.

investigate.text: Bloods for systemic infection, glucose and HbA1c.
Pelvic MRI or endoanal ultrasound for recurrent, complex, deep or Crohn's-related sepsis.
CT for suspected Fournier's gangrene only if it does not delay theatre.
Biopsy and further work-up of an atypical fissure or chronic non-healing wound.

resuscitate.text: Thrombosed external haemorrhoid beyond the early window: non-operative care with analgesia, stool softeners and topical agents; the pain usually settles within days.
Acute anal fissure: fibre, fluids, sitz baths and topical analgesia first.
Chronic fissure: topical calcium channel blocker or nitrate as first-line medical therapy; calcium channel blockers have fewer headaches.

definitive.text: Drain the abscess through an incision close to the anal verge to keep any fistula tract short; avoid aggressive probing for an internal opening in acute inflamed tissue.
If a simple low fistula is obvious at drainage, an experienced surgeon may lay it open; otherwise place a loose seton or defer and reassess.
Chronic fissure refractory to medical therapy: botulinum toxin, or lateral internal sphincterotomy after discussing the risk to continence.
Pilonidal disease after the acute phase: definitive excision or a minimally invasive technique; off-midline closure is preferred when closing primarily.
Fournier's gangrene: radical debridement of all non-viable tissue with planned re-look within 24 to 48 hours; diversion only when faecal soiling makes wound care impossible.

escalate.text: Senior surgeon and critical care immediately for suspected Fournier's gangrene; urology for scrotal involvement.
Colorectal surgeon for recurrent, complex, high or Crohn's-related fistula and for any sepsis in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease.
Gastroenterology for suspected Crohn's disease; infectious diseases for suspected tuberculosis or HIV.

notes: Perianal sepsis is a pus problem, not an antibiotic problem. The commonest error is a course of oral antibiotics that lets the abscess track deeper.
A substantial minority of anorectal abscesses, often quoted as about a third, go on to a fistula. Warn the patient at drainage, and do not create a fistula by probing.
The perineum of a diabetic patient can look unremarkable while the infection spreads beneath it. Feel for crepitus and do not trust a quiet skin.
